title: Module 1 - Governance, Risk, and Compliance - Part 11

questions.learningObjective: Given a set of organizational security requirements, implement the appropriate governance components.
questions.stem: An emergency firewall change skipped review and later broke a regulated data feed. Which root cause is most important to address?

choices.A: Operationalize the policy into a procedure with required steps, evidence, approvals, and tests
choices.B: Govern staging data with minimization, masking/tokenization, access limits, and retention rules
choices.C: Use a GRC tool or evidence register that maps controls, owners, exceptions, tests, and obligations
choices.D: Build a RACI that separates recommendation, consultation, approval, execution, and evidence ownership
choices.E: Require change governance: risk classification, emergency approval, rollback evidence, and post-implementation review

questions.explanation: This is a change and configuration governance problem. The cue—an emergency change bypassed review and broke a regulated feed—points to a process that keeps emergency agility but still produces accountable, reviewable change. That is exactly E: classify emergency changes, require rollback evidence, and run a post-implementation review. The other options are real controls, but none directly closes the emergency-change gap.

whyWrong.A: Procedures operationalize policy in general; they do not specifically govern emergency changes or require rollback and post-change review.
whyWrong.B: Staging data governance protects test data, not the change process that failed here.
whyWrong.C: A GRC evidence register tracks controls broadly; it does not classify or control emergency changes.
whyWrong.D: A RACI assigns decision ownership but does not impose emergency-change classification or rollback evidence.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.1: Given a set of organizational security requirements, implement the appropriate governance components.

whyCorrect.E: It targets the actual gap—accountable emergency change—and leaves rollback and review evidence a reviewer can check later.

questions.learningObjective: Summarize the information security challenges associated with artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.
questions.stem: Employees paste regulated case notes into an AI assistant to speed up summaries. Weighing security value, operational burden, and evidence quality, which option is most defensible?

choices.A: Require model/version governance, evaluation evidence, change notification, and rollback criteria
choices.B: Treat model output as advisory and validate it against telemetry, policy, and human approval thresholds
choices.C: Limit tool permissions, isolate untrusted content, and require approval for high-impact actions
choices.D: Update detection, awareness, and response for AI-enabled social engineering at scale
choices.E: Define approved data classes, retention rules, logging, and redaction controls for AI use

questions.explanation: AI assistants create new ways for regulated data to leak and be retained. When users feed sensitive content into a model, the core control is governing what data is allowed in and how prompts and outputs are handled. That is E: classify allowed inputs, redact sensitive fields, and audit prompt/output handling. The other options address different AI risks (supply chain, output trust, injection, adversary use), not the data-exposure path in this scenario.

whyWrong.A: Model and version governance addresses supply-chain change, not what regulated data users paste in.
whyWrong.B: Validating output reliability does not stop sensitive data from entering or being retained by the model.
whyWrong.C: Tool permissioning and injection isolation address action abuse, not the data-exposure path here.
whyWrong.D: Detection and awareness target AI-enabled attackers, not internal data leakage into the assistant.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.5: Summarize the information security challenges associated with artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.

whyCorrect.E: It directly controls AI data leakage and retention by classifying allowed inputs and auditing how prompts and outputs are handled.

questions.learningObjective: Given a set of organizational security requirements, implement the appropriate governance components.
questions.topic: policy, standard, procedure, and guideline separation
questions.stem: A board-approved privileged access policy must be turned into repeatable engineering work instructions. Which control objective should the reviewer apply?

choices.A: Operationalize the policy into a procedure with required steps, evidence, approvals, and tests
choices.B: Build a RACI that separates recommendation, consultation, approval, execution, and evidence ownership
choices.C: Govern staging data with minimization, masking/tokenization, access limits, and retention rules
choices.D: Require change governance: risk classification, emergency approval, rollback evidence, and post-implementation review
choices.E: Use a GRC tool or evidence register that maps controls, owners, exceptions, tests, and obligations

questions.explanation: Policies state intent; procedures turn that intent into repeatable, testable execution. Converting a policy into work instructions is the defining job of a procedure, so A is correct—it defines the steps, approvers, evidence, and tests that make the policy actually executable. The other choices govern different artifacts (decision ownership, staging data, change, GRC evidence).

whyWrong.B: A RACI assigns who decides; it does not write the repeatable steps the policy needs.
whyWrong.C: Staging data governance is unrelated to operationalizing an access policy.
whyWrong.D: Change governance controls modifications, not the conversion of policy into procedure.
whyWrong.E: A GRC register tracks evidence across obligations; it does not author the work instructions.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.1: Given a set of organizational security requirements, implement the appropriate governance components.

whyCorrect.A: A procedure is the artifact that translates policy intent into repeatable steps, approvers, and evidence.

questions.learningObjective: Summarize the information security challenges associated with artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.
questions.stem: Analysts want AI recommendations to auto-close incidents when confidence is high. Which items separate a defensible answer from a superficial one? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Model output is probabilistic, not authoritative evidence, so it should be treated as advisory and validated before driving action. A defensible answer keeps the controls that make that validation real: showing the evidence the model used (A), requiring corroborating signals (B), and tracking false positives (E). Choices about hardening reporting workflows (C) and AI input classification (D) belong to other topics and do not validate output reliability.

whyWrong.C: Hardening reporting workflows targets AI-enabled adversary activity, not output validation.
whyWrong.D: Classifying allowed inputs addresses data leakage, not whether the output is reliable.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.5: Summarize the information security challenges associated with artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.

whyCorrect.A: Showing the evidence the model relied on makes its recommendation auditable instead of a black box.
whyCorrect.B: Requiring corroborating signals prevents acting on a single probabilistic output.
whyCorrect.E: Tracking false positives measures whether the model is reliable enough to trust over time.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how compliance affects information security strategies.
questions.stem: A product roadmap plans to collect device identifiers, support notes, and behavior telemetry for a new personalization feature. Which root cause is most important to address?

choices.A: Design controls around applicable healthcare, privacy, retention, access, and reporting obligations
choices.B: Adjust architecture and governance to meet residency, processing, and contractual restrictions
choices.C: Distinguish audits, assessments, and certifications by scope, period, criteria, and current control evidence
choices.D: Apply purpose limitation, minimization, consent/notice where needed, retention, and subject-rights handling
choices.E: Map metrics to a recognized framework and show risk, control performance, exceptions, and trend evidence

questions.explanation: Privacy is a data-lifecycle design constraint, not a notice you bolt on after launch. When a feature collects personal data, the root issue is governing why and how much is collected and for how long. That is D: validate purpose, minimize collection, and define retention, access, and subject rights. The other options address adjacent compliance topics but skip the lifecycle controls this feature needs.

whyWrong.A: Sector-specific (e.g., healthcare) obligations are broader than the lifecycle controls this collection requires.
whyWrong.B: Residency and processing-location rules address where data lives, not whether collection is justified and minimized.
whyWrong.C: Audit and certification evidence proves controls operate; it does not constrain data collection.
whyWrong.E: Reporting metrics communicate posture; they do not enforce purpose limitation or minimization.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.3: Explain how compliance affects information security strategies.

whyCorrect.D: It applies privacy as a lifecycle design rule—purpose, minimization, retention, and subject rights—before the feature ships.

questions.learningObjective: Summarize the information security challenges associated with artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.
questions.topic: AI supply chain and model governance
questions.stem: A vendor model is updated silently and changes its detection recommendations. Which root cause is most important to address?

choices.A: Treat model output as advisory and validate it against telemetry, policy, and human approval thresholds
choices.B: Limit tool permissions, isolate untrusted content, and require approval for high-impact actions
choices.C: Require model/version governance, evaluation evidence, change notification, and rollback criteria
choices.D: Update detection, awareness, and response for AI-enabled social engineering at scale
choices.E: Define approved data classes, retention rules, logging, and redaction controls for AI use

questions.explanation: An AI model is a critical dependency, so it needs the same lifecycle governance as any other—versioning, change notification, evaluation, and rollback. A silent vendor update that shifts behavior is the classic supply-chain gap, answered by C: record model versions and define rollback triggers. The other options address output trust, injection, adversary use, or data leakage, not uncontrolled model change.

whyWrong.A: Validating output reliability does not detect or control an unannounced model change.
whyWrong.B: Tool permissioning limits actions, not silent model updates.
whyWrong.D: Detection and awareness target attackers, not vendor model drift.
whyWrong.E: Data-class and retention controls address leakage, not version governance.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.5: Summarize the information security challenges associated with artificial intelligence (AI) adoption.

whyCorrect.C: It governs the AI supply chain by tracking versions, requiring change notice, and defining rollback when behavior shifts.

questions.learningObjective: Given a set of organizational security requirements, implement the appropriate governance components.
questions.stem: An emergency firewall change skipped review and later broke a regulated data feed. Which elements belong in the design package? (Select all that apply.)

choices.E: Document workflow steps and required evidence

questions.explanation: Change and configuration governance keeps emergency speed while staying accountable. The pieces that close this gap are classifying emergency changes (D), requiring rollback plans (A), and performing a post-change review (B). Masking data (C) is staging-data governance, and documenting workflow steps (E) is a procedure concern—both useful elsewhere but not the emergency-change control.

whyWrong.C: Masking or tokenizing fields is staging-data governance, not change control.
whyWrong.E: Documenting workflow steps is a procedure artifact, not an emergency-change control.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.1: Given a set of organizational security requirements, implement the appropriate governance components.

whyCorrect.A: A rollback plan lets the team back out or recover from a failed emergency change, limiting how long the impact persists.
whyCorrect.B: A post-change review captures impact and lessons, turning the bypass into accountable evidence.
whyCorrect.D: Classifying emergency changes sets the risk-based approval path so review is not simply skipped.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how compliance affects information security strategies.
questions.stem: The board wants a cybersecurity scorecard that supports regulatory reporting and investment decisions. Which target-state design is most complete and defensible?

choices.A: Apply purpose limitation, minimization, consent/notice where needed, retention, and subject-rights handling
choices.B: Design controls around applicable healthcare, privacy, retention, access, and reporting obligations
choices.C: Adjust architecture and governance to meet residency, processing, and contractual restrictions
choices.D: Map metrics to a recognized framework and show risk, control performance, exceptions, and trend evidence
choices.E: Distinguish audits, assessments, and certifications by scope, period, criteria, and current control evidence

questions.explanation: Board reporting needs decision-useful evidence tied to recognized control objectives, not raw activity counts. That means mapping metrics to a framework and showing risk, control performance, exceptions, and trends—choice D. The other options are valid compliance or privacy controls, but they do not produce the framework-aligned scorecard the board asked for.

whyWrong.A: Privacy lifecycle controls protect data; they are not an executive reporting framework.
whyWrong.B: Sector-specific compliance design does not produce a board-level scorecard.
whyWrong.C: Residency and processing controls address data location, not reporting metrics.
whyWrong.E: Audit and certification distinctions describe assurance types, not the scorecard itself.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.3: Explain how compliance affects information security strategies.

whyCorrect.D: It frames metrics against a recognized framework and surfaces risk, performance, exceptions, and trends for decisions.

questions.learningObjective: Given a set of organizational security requirements, perform risk management activities.
questions.stem: Leadership wants to compare ransomware-outage risk against payment-fraud risk using both expected loss and strategic impact. Which approach best addresses the issue?

choices.A: Apply compensating controls, document residual risk, and obtain accountable risk acceptance
choices.B: Run a business impact analysis and turn impact tolerance into recovery and continuity requirements
choices.C: Assess data, model, output, automation, privacy, and accountability risks before operational use
choices.D: Combine quantitative estimates with qualitative business, safety, legal, and reputation factors
choices.E: Review contractual duties, access scope, logging, subprocessors, breach notification, and offboarding controls

questions.explanation: Comparing one risk in dollars and another in strategic terms needs both numeric and contextual evidence. A quantitative-only or qualitative-only view would miss half the picture, so the answer is D: pair expected-loss estimates with business, safety, legal, and reputation factors and state the assumptions. The other options are valid risk activities but do not blend both lenses for this comparison.

whyWrong.A: Compensating controls and risk acceptance treat a risk; they do not analyze and compare two risks.
whyWrong.B: A business impact analysis sizes recovery needs, not a quantitative-plus-qualitative risk comparison.
whyWrong.C: AI usage risk assessment is the wrong domain for ransomware-versus-fraud comparison.
whyWrong.E: Third-party risk review covers vendor obligations, not this internal risk comparison.

sources: CAS005 LO 1.2: Given a set of organizational security requirements, perform risk management activities.

whyCorrect.D: It blends quantitative loss estimates with qualitative impact factors, the only way to compare these two risks fairly.
